newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries aloft at noon, NAPM, technicals lift.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries aloft at noon, NAPM, technicals lift.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury markets were cheering at noon, after the National Association of Purchasing Management index provided more evidence that healthy economic growth was not fanning worrisome inflation.
"It's just the best of all worlds scenario continuing" for Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, said Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co Inc.
"He's seeing strong indications of continued strong growth but no evidence of rising price pressures in this stage of the cycle," he added.
The T-bond's price jumped, ending early softness, after the NAPM said its index stood at 55.7 for June.
Much of the advance was technically driven, fueled by stop-loss buying above 111-16/32 in the September bond futures contract, analysts said.
The 30-year bond was up 18/32 around midday, standing at 98-16/32 with a yield of 6.74 percent.
The national purchasers number, though lower than May's 57.1 reading and forecasts of 56.4, was still well above the 50.0 boom/bust threshold and was the second highest posted this year.
Moreover, the widely watched prices component fell to 48.1 percent from 48.4 in May.

Fears that NAPM would be higher than forecast were sparked by a string of regional purchasers' reports on Monday -- notably the Chicagoland business barometer -- which showed economic activity improved significanly in June.

"The market was fearing a fairly healthy NAPM report. It ended up being slightly lower and Treasuries have taken off, some stops were hit and they largely moved to new highs on technical factors," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at Standard and Poor's MMS.

A sharp 1.8 percent drop in construction spending in May, the largest decline since January 1994, also supported the market, experts said. The construction number for April was revised up to a 0.3 percent rise from a 1.0 percent drop.
"We don't want to short change construction spending," said Mike Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.

"It implied that construction activity for the second quarter as a whole is probably going to be down, which means this area was a drag on the economy ... So it was, I thought, an important report," Moran added.

The Federal Open Market Committee starts its two-day meeting this afternoon. The market has already priced in steady rates and the gathering should have little bearing on trade at least until policy-makers wrap it up on Wednesday.
In a Reuters poll of 36 economists, all forecast no change in interest rates, expecting the target for the fed funds rate will remain at 5.5 percent, where it has stood since March 25.

In the meantime, the market will shift its gaze beyond various vehicle sales data and the Redbook index on retail sales from last week later Tuesday, and start zeroing in on Thursday's key jobs report from June, analysts said.
Non-farm payrolls are expected to gain 222,000 after increasing 138,000 in May. The unemployment rate is seen remaining at 4.8 percent in June.
In other early afternoon dealings, the 10-year note was up 13/32 at 101-9/32, with a yield of 6.45 percent. The five-year note was up 4/32 at 99-21/32 yielding 6.33 percent.
Three-month bills were off two basis points at 5.10 percent and six-month bills were down one basis point at 5.12 percent.
((--Alden Bentley, New York Treasury Desk, 212 859 1667))
